almaco-jack.name: Almaco jack
almaco-jack.description: A deep-bodied, olive to silver-gray jack with tall, sickle-shaped dorsal and anal fins and a dark band slanting from the eye to the top of the head.
almaco-jack.tip: Look out into the blue along walls and over deep wrecks. Small groups swing in to look at divers, so hold still and let them pass close.

arrow-blenny.name: Arrow blenny
arrow-blenny.description: A pencil-thin, see-through orange blenny with a long pointed snout and a row of black spots near the tail, often hanging with its tail curled into a hook.
arrow-blenny.tip: Look along walls and under ledges, mostly below 15 meters. Watch the curled tail; it is cocked to dart at passing plankton.

arrow-crab.name: Yellowline arrow crab
arrow-crab.description: A spider of a crab, all legs and a needle nose, walking the reef at night.
arrow-crab.tip: Sweep a light slowly across a sponge face; the legs catch the beam first.

atlantic-common-octopus.name: Atlantic common octopus
atlantic-common-octopus.description: A large, reddish-brown octopus with bumpy skin that turns pale or mottled in a blink, near rubble and sand.
atlantic-common-octopus.tip: Look for a den ringed with empty shells; wait at a distance and it may come to the entrance.

atlantic-longarm-octopus.name: Atlantic longarm octopus
atlantic-longarm-octopus.description: A small, sand-colored octopus with arms several times its body length, crawling over open sand at night.
atlantic-longarm-octopus.tip: Sweep a light over open sand on a night dive; when disturbed it swims off flat, like a flounder.

atlantic-spadefish.name: Atlantic spadefish
atlantic-spadefish.description: Tall silver discs banded in black, drifting over a wreck in a slow crowd.
atlantic-spadefish.tip: They circle rather than flee. Stay low and the whole school will come around again.

atlantic-spotted-dolphin.name: Atlantic spotted dolphin
atlantic-spotted-dolphin.description: A stocky dolphin whose adults are covered in dark and pale spots; the young are plain gray.
atlantic-spotted-dolphin.tip: Let them come to you. Stay calm and level in the water, and never reach out.

azure-vase-sponge.name: Azure vase sponge
azure-vase-sponge.description: A fluted violet-pink cup that almost glows against the reef face.
azure-vase-sponge.tip: Get low and shoot up into the cup. The color only reads with light in it.

balloonfish.name: Balloonfish
balloonfish.description: A spiny puffer with long spines and copper eyes, resting under a ledge by day.
balloonfish.tip: Never provoke one into inflating. It is a stress response, not a trick.

banded-butterflyfish.name: Banded butterflyfish
banded-butterflyfish.description: A white disc crossed by four dark bands, almost always in a pair.
banded-butterflyfish.tip: Watch one pair for a minute. They work a patch of reef together and circle back.

banded-coral-shrimp.name: Banded coral shrimp
banded-coral-shrimp.description: Red-and-white candy stripes with white antennae twice its own length.
banded-coral-shrimp.tip: The waving antennae are the advertisement, so look for those, not the body.

bandtail-puffer.name: Bandtail puffer
bandtail-puffer.description: A small mottled puffer with a row of dark blotches along the belly, low on the sand.
bandtail-puffer.tip: Sits still on the bottom and lets you pass. Sweep the sand at the reef edge for it.

bar-jack.name: Bar jack
bar-jack.description: A silver jack with one electric-blue stripe down the back, often shadowing a ray.
bar-jack.tip: When you find a stingray feeding, look just above it. A jack is usually riding along.

barred-cardinalfish.name: Barred cardinalfish
barred-cardinalfish.description: A small red fish with big eyes and two thin dark bars, one under the rear dorsal fin and one at the base of the tail.
barred-cardinalfish.tip: By day it hides deep in crevices. On a night dive it hovers in the open, so keep your light off its eyes.

barred-hamlet.name: Barred hamlet
barred-hamlet.description: A small tan bass with a dark saddle amidships, hanging just off the coral.
barred-hamlet.tip: Hamlets hold a spot and watch you, so approach one slowly instead of sweeping the reef.

batwing-coral-crab.name: Batwing coral crab
batwing-coral-crab.description: A big, smooth, brick-red crab speckled with cream, with pale bat-wing shapes on its shell.
batwing-coral-crab.tip: Look into reef holes on a night dive; it hides by day and holds still in your light.

beaded-sea-cucumber.name: Beaded sea cucumber
beaded-sea-cucumber.description: A long, soft, see-through cucumber banded like a string of beads, stretching a meter or more over the reef at night.
beaded-sea-cucumber.tip: Look for it on night dives; its skin is sticky, so watch rather than touch.

bearded-fireworm.name: Bearded fireworm
bearded-fireworm.description: A thick, segmented worm, green to orange, with tufts of white bristles down each side and red gills along its back.
bearded-fireworm.tip: Never touch one: the white bristles break off in your skin and burn for hours.

beaugregory.name: Beaugregory
beaugregory.description: Juveniles are blue above and yellow below with a blue-ringed black spot on the back fin; adults fade to dusky brown with a yellow tail.
beaugregory.tip: Check the shallow seagrass and rubble. It guards a small patch and will nip at a diver who lingers too long.

belted-cardinalfish.name: Belted cardinalfish
belted-cardinalfish.description: A small orange-red cardinalfish with a dark bar under the rear dorsal fin and two dark bands close together at the tail base that read as one belt.
belted-cardinalfish.tip: Hides in crevices by day. On a night dive, sweep your light along ledges and keep it moving.

belted-sandfish.name: Belted sandfish
belted-sandfish.description: A small mottled brown bass with a black blotch on the back fin and a white patch on the belly, on rocks and jetties.
belted-sandfish.tip: A Florida and Gulf of Mexico fish. Scan rocky ledges and jetty boulders, where it perches and watches you back.

bermuda-chub.name: Bermuda chub
bermuda-chub.description: An oval silver-gray fish lined with faint bronze stripes, cruising in schools above shallow reefs.
bermuda-chub.tip: Look up from the reef top. Schools pass in the water column and often swim close to curious divers on their own.

bicolor-damselfish.name: Bicolor damselfish
bicolor-damselfish.description: A small damselfish split in two: dark brown in front, white behind, often with a yellow wash where the halves meet.
bicolor-damselfish.tip: Each one keeps a patch of reef slope. Hold still nearby and watch it chase off fish many times its size.

black-coral.name: Black coral
black-coral.description: Feathery gray-green bushes on deep walls; the black is the skeleton inside.
black-coral.tip: Slow-growing and protected nearly everywhere. Keep fins and gauges well off the wall.

black-durgon.name: Black durgon
black-durgon.description: Black at a glance, and blue-green with bright seams once light reaches it.
black-durgon.tip: Put a light on one. The color it looks at ten meters is not the color it is.

black-grouper.name: Black grouper
black-grouper.description: A big, dark, rectangular grouper that holds station off the reef edge.
black-grouper.tip: Keep your distance and it stays; swim straight at it and the dive is over.

black-hamlet.name: Black hamlet
black-hamlet.description: A hamlet that is solid blue-black from nose to tail, sometimes with a faint blue sheen on the fins.
black-hamlet.tip: Common close to the coral at moderate depth. Hold still and it comes back to its patch.

black-margate.name: Black margate
black-margate.description: A big, high-backed grunt in dark gray, each scale with a dark center, and a paler head.
black-margate.tip: It hangs under ledges and in the shade of coral heads. Approach low and slow and it will often hold still for you.

black-sea-rod.name: Black sea rod
black-sea-rod.description: A bushy gorgonian with dark brown to black branches, mostly in one plane, fuzzy with brown polyps when they are out.
black-sea-rod.tip: Check the branches for flamingo tongues and other small snails. Look without touching the rod.

black-tunicate.name: Black tunicate
black-tunicate.description: A smooth, glossy black sac about the size of a fist, with two openings, stuck to rock, pilings or mangrove roots.
black-tunicate.tip: Watch its two siphons pump water, and keep your hands off; touched, it clenches and squirts.

blackbar-soldierfish.name: Blackbar soldierfish
blackbar-soldierfish.description: Red, big-eyed and nocturnal, hanging upside-down inside caves by day.
blackbar-soldierfish.tip: Bring a light into an overhang and look at the ceiling, not the floor.

blackcap-basslet.name: Blackcap basslet
blackcap-basslet.description: A finger-length violet fish with a black band running from its snout back along the top of the dorsal fin.
blackcap-basslet.tip: Look deeper than the royal grammas, usually past 20 meters, hanging belly-to-rock under overhangs on the wall.

blacknose-shark.name: Blacknose shark
blacknose-shark.description: A small, slim gray shark with a short, rounded snout marked by a dark smudge at the tip, and no other bold marks on the fins.
blacknose-shark.tip: Usually met over sand and shallow reef, mostly in warm months. On a provisioned dive, follow the crew’s briefing to the letter; anywhere else, treat it as an unplanned encounter: stay calm, keep your hands in and let it pass.

blacktip-shark.name: Blacktip shark
blacktip-shark.description: A slim, fast gray-bronze shark with black tips on most fins, notably the second dorsal and the tail.
blacktip-shark.tip: Met in shallow water, more in winter and spring around the Bahamas and Florida. Stay calm, keep your hands in and let it pass.

blade-fire-coral.name: Blade fire coral
blade-fire-coral.description: Flat mustard-tan blades with pale edges, standing in rows on the shallow reef crest where the surge runs.
blade-fire-coral.tip: It stings on contact. Give it a wide berth in surge, where a wave can push you into it.

blue-angelfish.name: Blue angelfish
blue-angelfish.description: A blue-gray angelfish with yellow-rimmed fins and a blue tail with a yellow edge. It has no dark crown on the forehead, which sets it apart from the queen.
blue-angelfish.tip: Check the forehead and the tail before you call it a queen. It feeds on sponges, so look where they grow thick.

blue-chromis.name: Blue chromis
blue-chromis.description: Small electric-blue slivers hanging in open water just above the coral.
blue-chromis.tip: Look up and out from the reef rather than down; they feed in the water column.

blue-dartfish.name: Blue dartfish
blue-dartfish.description: A slim, pale-blue fish with a long, low dorsal fin and fins thinly edged in red, hovering in pairs over a burrow in sand or rubble.
blue-dartfish.tip: Usually deeper than 20 meters on sandy slopes. Settle low a few body lengths away and wait; a pair dives into the burrow at any sudden move.

blue-parrotfish.name: Blue parrotfish
blue-parrotfish.description: A big parrotfish that is powder blue all over, with large adults growing a squared hump over the beak.
blue-parrotfish.tip: Look over sand and rubble between reef patches, where groups graze on the move. Listen for the crunch of their beaks on the rock.

blue-runner.name: Blue runner
blue-runner.description: A sleek jack, olive to bluish-green on the back and silver below, with a small black spot on the gill cover.
blue-runner.tip: Schools move fast along the reef edge and around wrecks. Watch the open water rather than chasing them.

blue-tang.name: Blue tang
blue-tang.description: A deep blue oval with a bright scalpel at the tail; juveniles are yellow.
blue-tang.tip: Hover rather than chase. A loose group grazes past you on its own.

bluebell-tunicate.name: Bluebell tunicate
bluebell-tunicate.description: Clusters of small, see-through blue to violet bells, each with a pale ring at the mouth, on sea rods and rock.
bluebell-tunicate.tip: Get close and look through the bells; each one is a separate animal filtering the water.

bluehead-wrasse.name: Bluehead wrasse
bluehead-wrasse.description: Yellow youngsters and blue-headed adults, darting nose-down over the coral.
bluehead-wrasse.tip: Find a cleaning station and stay still; they come to you.

bluelip-parrotfish.name: Bluelip parrotfish
bluelip-parrotfish.description: A slim parrotfish the length of a hand in seagrass and rubble. Most are pale pink, and males add blue lips and washes of green and gold.
bluelip-parrotfish.tip: Swim the seagrass edge slowly. At night it buries itself in the sand inside a mucus cocoon, so do not dig.

bluestriped-grunt.name: Bluestriped grunt
bluestriped-grunt.description: Yellow flanks ruled with electric blue lines, in loose crowds under ledges.
bluestriped-grunt.tip: Look into the shade under overhangs. A whole school can sit out the day there.

bluethroat-pikeblenny.name: Bluethroat pikeblenny
bluethroat-pikeblenny.description: A pencil-thin blenny with a long, pike-like jaw that sits in a hole in the sand or rubble with only its head showing. Males flare a blue throat and a dark-spotted fin.
bluethroat-pikeblenny.tip: Look for a small head in a hole in the bottom, then wait. It ducks back out of sight if you lean in, so shoot from a little way off.

boga.name: Boga
boga.description: A slim, fork-tailed fish, blue-green above and silver below with thin gold lines, streaming in schools in midwater over the reef.
boga.tip: Look up from the reef top. The schools turn as one and come close if you hang still in the water column.

bonefish.name: Bonefish
bonefish.description: A slim, silver, torpedo-shaped fish with a blunt snout and a forked tail, tailing over sand and seagrass flats.
bonefish.tip: Look on shallow flats and mangrove edges, often in small groups. Stay back and move slowly; they spook at a splash.

bottlenose-dolphin.name: Bottlenose dolphin
bottlenose-dolphin.description: Usually a surface encounter from the boat, occasionally a pass underwater.
bottlenose-dolphin.tip: Never chase. Stay where you are, and they decide whether it’s a meeting.

boulder-brain-coral.name: Boulder brain coral
boulder-brain-coral.description: Big brain-coral boulders, some taller than a diver, with wide valleys and a fine groove running along the top of each ridge.
boulder-brain-coral.tip: Find the groove on the ridge top and you have this species. Settle beside it, never on it.

boulder-star-coral.name: Boulder star coral
boulder-star-coral.description: Stacked columns with rounded tops, one of the reef’s main frame-builders.
boulder-star-coral.tip: Much of the reef you are swimming over is this. It took centuries to reach that size.

branching-anemone.name: Branching anemone
branching-anemone.description: A brown tuft of branching arms with pale, bead-like tips, spreading out of a crevice by day.
branching-anemone.tip: Its sting is strong, so keep your hands off the reef and your fins up near a crevice.

branching-tube-sponge.name: Branching tube sponge
branching-tube-sponge.description: Knobby lumps and short tubes in yellow, purple, or a mottled mix of both, one colony rarely matching the next.
branching-tube-sponge.tip: Go by the bumpy surface, not the color. Where it is scraped it darkens toward purple, so keep fins well clear.

branching-vase-sponge.name: Branching vase sponge
branching-vase-sponge.description: Clusters of purple-gray tubes with rough walls, leaning away from the current.
branching-vase-sponge.tip: Look into the tubes. Brittle stars and small gobies live down inside them.

brazilian-reef-octopus.name: Brazilian reef octopus
brazilian-reef-octopus.description: A reef octopus that hunts in daylight, often out in the open, shifting from red-brown with pale spots to a mottled white as it moves.
brazilian-reef-octopus.tip: Keep your distance and let it hunt. Crowd it and it flattens, changes color and slips into the nearest hole.

bridled-goby.name: Bridled goby
bridled-goby.description: A pale, sand-colored goby speckled with small dark marks, resting on sand and rubble at the edge of the reef.
bridled-goby.tip: It vanishes against the sand until it hops. Hold still near a sand patch and wait for the next short dash.

broadstripe-goby.name: Broadstripe goby
broadstripe-goby.description: A small cleaner goby with a wide pale stripe from snout to tail between dark bands, perched on coral or in a sponge.
broadstripe-goby.tip: A fish holding still over a coral head with its mouth open is being cleaned. Watch from a meter back.

brown-chromis.name: Brown chromis
brown-chromis.description: Olive-brown slivers feeding in open water, often mixed in with the blue ones.
brown-chromis.tip: Where you find blue chromis, look again. The brown ones feed in the same cloud.

brown-encrusting-octopus-sponge.name: Brown encrusting octopus sponge
brown-encrusting-octopus-sponge.description: Orange-brown to rust crusts and low lobes spread over rock, raised into small volcano-shaped openings with pale rims.
brown-encrusting-octopus-sponge.tip: Tell it from other orange crusts by the volcanoes. Watch from above rather than resting on the rock it covers.

brown-tube-sponge.name: Brown tube sponge
brown-tube-sponge.description: Clusters of tan to brown tubes, the outer wall studded with small cone-shaped bumps and round openings.
brown-tube-sponge.tip: Look into the tops of the tubes for gobies and small shrimp. Keep your gauges from swinging into them.

bull-shark.name: Bull shark
bull-shark.description: A stocky gray shark with a short, blunt snout, small eyes and no markings on its fins.
bull-shark.tip: On a provisioned shark dive, follow the operator’s briefing exactly; anywhere else, treat it as an unplanned encounter: stay calm, keep it in view and end the dive.

butter-hamlet.name: Butter hamlet
butter-hamlet.description: A pale, butter-colored hamlet with a black saddle at the base of the tail and often a dark spot on the snout ringed in blue.
butter-hamlet.tip: Hamlets keep to their patch of reef. Find one and wait, and it will circle back past you.

caesar-grunt.name: Caesar grunt
caesar-grunt.description: A gray grunt lined with bronze-yellow stripes, with dark fins and tail, resting with other grunts under ledges.
caesar-grunt.tip: The dark fins pick it out of a mixed grunt school. Watch from outside the ledge so the group stays settled.

cannonball-jelly.name: Cannonball jelly
cannonball-jelly.description: A firm, round bell, milky white with a brown rim, often drifting in big swarms near the coast.
cannonball-jelly.tip: Its sting is mild, but keep clear of the arms under the bell and give a swarm room.

caribbean-neon-goby.name: Caribbean neon goby
caribbean-neon-goby.description: A tiny dark goby with an electric-blue stripe from eye to tail and no mark on the snout, cleaning fish on coral heads from Belize to Honduras.
caribbean-neon-goby.tip: Stop near a coral head where bigger fish hang still with mouths and gills open. The gobies are working them over.

caribbean-reef-octopus.name: Caribbean reef octopus
caribbean-reef-octopus.description: Blue-green and shape-shifting, out hunting across the reef after dark.
caribbean-reef-octopus.tip: A night dive doubles your odds. Keep the light off its eyes and it stays out.

caribbean-reef-shark.name: Caribbean reef shark
caribbean-reef-shark.description: A classic gray requiem shark that patrols the reef edge in open water.
caribbean-reef-shark.tip: Stay calm and level, keep the group together, and watch it rather than follow it.

caribbean-reef-squid.name: Caribbean reef squid
caribbean-reef-squid.description: A small squadron holding formation in mid-water, colors running across them.
caribbean-reef-squid.tip: Approach slowly and they hold. They are talking to each other in those colors.

cayman-cleaning-goby.name: Cayman cleaning goby
cayman-cleaning-goby.description: A tiny cleaner goby found only around the Cayman Islands, with a yellow V on the snout that runs back as a thin yellow line beside a pale stripe.
cayman-cleaning-goby.tip: Watch the top of a coral head or sponge where fish line up. Stay still and the gobies keep working.

cayman-sponge-goby.name: Cayman sponge goby
cayman-sponge-goby.description: A small dusky goby with a yellow stripe from eye to tail that fades bluish-white toward the back, and no mark on the snout.
cayman-sponge-goby.tip: Look inside and around large tube and barrel sponges in the Cayman Islands. Peer in without touching the sponge.

cero.name: Cero
cero.description: A long silver mackerel with a bronze stripe from the pectoral fin to the tail, and rows of gold dashes above and below it.
cero.tip: Watch the blue off the reef edge. It cruises past alone or in twos, and comes closer if you hold still.

chain-moray.name: Chain moray
chain-moray.description: Dark brown printed with a yellow chain-link pattern, and short for a moray.
chain-moray.tip: Hunts crabs in the shallows by day, sometimes half out of the water. Look shallow. Keep your hands out of the holes.

chalk-bass.name: Chalk bass
chalk-bass.description: A small sea bass in blue and salmon bars, hovering in loose groups low over rubble at the foot of deeper reefs.
chalk-bass.tip: Look below about 15 meters where reef meets rubble. Stay low and the group settles back down around you.

channel-clinging-crab.name: Channel clinging crab
channel-clinging-crab.description: A dinner-plate crab wedged into a crevice, out only when the lights go down.
channel-clinging-crab.tip: Check the deep cracks in a wall. You see the claws before the animal.

cherubfish.name: Cherubfish
cherubfish.description: A thumb-sized pygmy angelfish, deep blue with a yellow-orange face and a blue ring around the eye.
cherubfish.tip: It darts between holes in rubble and coral, often deeper than 15 meters. Stop beside its patch and it reappears.

christmas-tree-hydroid.name: Christmas tree hydroid
christmas-tree-hydroid.description: Dark, feathery stems with side branches tipped in tiny white polyps, like a fern hung with lights.
christmas-tree-hydroid.tip: It stings bare skin on contact, so admire it from a fin’s length away.

christmas-tree-worm.name: Christmas tree worm
christmas-tree-worm.description: Pairs of tiny colored spirals growing straight out of hard coral.
christmas-tree-worm.tip: Let your shadow cross one and every worm on the head vanishes at once. Then hold still and wait for them to reopen.

cleaning-goby.name: Cleaning goby
cleaning-goby.description: A tiny cleaner goby with a bright yellow V on the snout that runs into a wide white to yellow stripe, found in the Bahamas.
cleaning-goby.tip: Fish lining up on a coral head point you to its station. Settle beside it and let the queue carry on.

clown-wrasse.name: Clown wrasse
clown-wrasse.description: Young ones are white with a black stripe and a yellow back; terminal males are green with pink lines on the head and a dark spot on the side.
clown-wrasse.tip: Busy and quick over rubble and low reef. Pause beside one patch and the same few will keep circling past.

cobia.name: Cobia
cobia.description: A dark torpedo often mistaken for a shark, cruising past wrecks in open water.
cobia.tip: Look into the blue away from the structure, not only along it.

cocoa-damselfish.name: Cocoa damselfish
cocoa-damselfish.description: Blue above and yellow below with blue speckles, a dark spot on the back fin and another on top of the tail base.
cocoa-damselfish.tip: The spot on top of the tail base separates it from a young beaugregory. Look along low reef and rubble.

colon-goby.name: Colon goby
colon-goby.description: A small, see-through goby freckled in orange and brown, with two dark dots stacked at the base of the pectoral fin.
colon-goby.tip: It rests on coral and rubble out in the open. Get low and look for the two dots, which set it apart from its look-alikes.

common-sea-fan.name: Common sea fan
common-sea-fan.description: A purple lattice standing across the current like a window frame.
common-sea-fan.tip: They grow square to the surge, so a stand of fans tells you which way the water moves.

common-snook.name: Common snook
common-snook.description: A long silver fish with a sloping forehead, a jutting lower jaw and a bold black line from gill to tail.
common-snook.tip: Look in the shade of mangrove roots, jetties and inlets. It holds still in the current, so drift past slowly rather than swim at it.

coney.name: Coney
coney.description: A hand-length grouper that comes in red, brown or bright yellow, all one species.
coney.tip: Tucked into sponges and ledges. The yellow phase is the one people photograph.

corkscrew-anemone.name: Corkscrew anemone
corkscrew-anemone.description: Long tentacles ringed with pale spirals, always with something living in them.
corkscrew-anemone.tip: Check inside every one. Cleaner shrimp and juvenile fish shelter there in the day.

corky-sea-finger.name: Corky sea finger
corky-sea-finger.description: Thick upright fingers, purple-gray underneath, often shaggy with brown polyps that make the whole colony look furry.
corky-sea-finger.tip: Flamingo tongues graze on it, so it is a good place to find one. Watch from a hand’s width away.

cottonwick.name: Cottonwick
cottonwick.description: A silvery grunt with thin yellow stripes and a black band running from the back fin down into a black tail.
cottonwick.tip: The black back and tail stand out in a mixed grunt school. Look along the reef edge, where small groups drift in the open.

creole-wrasse.name: Creole wrasse
creole-wrasse.description: Violet fish streaming along the reef edge in long, fast trains.
creole-wrasse.tip: Hold position at the drop-off and let the train come past you.

creolefish.name: Creolefish
creolefish.description: A slim salmon-red sea bass with a forked tail, a row of pale spots along the back and an orange spot at the base of the pectoral fin.
creolefish.tip: Look out from the wall into blue water, where loose schools hang in the current picking off plankton.

crevalle-jack.name: Crevalle jack
crevalle-jack.description: A thick silver jack with a blunt, steep head, a black spot on the gill cover and yellowish fins underneath.
crevalle-jack.tip: Schools sweep in from open water to hunt bait along the reef edge. Keep an eye on the blue.

cubera-snapper.name: Cubera snapper
cubera-snapper.description: The biggest Caribbean snapper: heavy-jawed, gray, and usually alone on a wreck.
cubera-snapper.tip: Solitary and wary. If one lets you close, stop where you are rather than pressing on.

cushion-sea-star.name: Cushion sea star
cushion-sea-star.description: A fat orange star the size of a dinner plate, out on open sand and seagrass.
cushion-sea-star.tip: Leave it in the water. Lifting one for a photo is what kills them.

doctorfish.name: Doctorfish
doctorfish.description: A gray-brown surgeonfish ruled with about ten thin dark bars down its sides.
doctorfish.tip: Count the bars to tell it from the ocean surgeonfish. It often grazes in mixed schools with blue tangs.

dog-snapper.name: Dog snapper
dog-snapper.description: Bronze, with a pale triangle under the eye and two canines it is named for.
dog-snapper.tip: Holds station at the mouth of a swim-through. Look before you enter, not after.

donkey-dung-sea-cucumber.name: Donkey dung sea cucumber
donkey-dung-sea-cucumber.description: A heavy brown cucumber lying on open sand, processing it a mouthful at a time.
donkey-dung-sea-cucumber.tip: Leave it be. Handling one makes it shed its insides, which it may not survive.

dushia-flabellina.name: Dushia flabellina
dushia-flabellina.description: A slim white nudibranch with clusters of orange-red, white-tipped cerata along its back and long white tentacles.
dushia-flabellina.tip: Search the hydroids on rubble and wrecks slowly, and let your light bring out the red.

dusky-damselfish.name: Dusky damselfish
dusky-damselfish.description: Juveniles are blue with bright spots under an orange-red head and back; adults turn plain dusky brown.
dusky-damselfish.tip: A fierce gardener in shallow surge zones and rubble. Admire its patch from a fin’s length away and it will still chase you off.

dusky-squirrelfish.name: Dusky squirrelfish
dusky-squirrelfish.description: A small, dusky red squirrelfish with fine pale stripes and short spines, shorter and darker than the common squirrelfish.
dusky-squirrelfish.tip: Look into holes in shallow reef and rock. It stays tucked in by day, so let your light find it from a distance.

elkhorn-coral.name: Elkhorn coral
elkhorn-coral.description: Broad antler branches in the shallows, the classic Caribbean reef silhouette.
elkhorn-coral.tip: This is the shallowest part of most dives, so watch your fins above it.

encrusting-gorgonian.name: Encrusting gorgonian
encrusting-gorgonian.description: A thin mat spread over rock and dead coral, shaggy with long tan polyps that sway like a rug in the surge.
encrusting-gorgonian.tip: With polyps pulled in it looks like a smooth gray crust. Watch the same patch for a minute and they come back out.

feather-duster-worm.name: Magnificent feather duster
feather-duster-worm.description: A soft banded fan on a tube, retracting the instant a shadow crosses it.
feather-duster-worm.tip: Approach from downstream and stay out of its light; it feels you coming.

finger-coral.name: Finger coral
finger-coral.description: Stubby blunt fingers in low thickets, tan to pale purple, in shallow water.
finger-coral.tip: A nursery: look between the fingers for the smallest fish on the reef.

fingerprint-cyphoma.name: Fingerprint cyphoma
fingerprint-cyphoma.description: A thumbnail snail with a pale, smooth shell and a mantle patterned in fine, close-set lines like a fingerprint, grazing on sea fans.
fingerprint-cyphoma.tip: Search the sea fans and gorgonians, on the same branches where flamingo tongues feed. Look without touching; the pattern is living tissue.

fire-coral.name: Branching fire coral
fire-coral.description: Mustard-tan blades with pale tips, growing over anything that stops moving.
fire-coral.tip: Not a coral and it does sting. Learn the mustard color and keep clear.

flagfin-mojarra.name: Flagfin mojarra
flagfin-mojarra.description: A small, shiny silver mojarra with a black tip on the dorsal fin like a flag, feeding over shallow sand.
flagfin-mojarra.tip: Look in clear shallows over sand and seagrass, near mangroves and docks. Small groups dip their protruding mouths into the sand.

flame-box-crab.name: Flame box crab
flame-box-crab.description: A domed crab with purple-brown flame streaks, holding broad claws over its face like a shield.
flame-box-crab.tip: Look over open sand at night for a hump with eyes. It buries itself fast if you crowd it.

flamefish.name: Flamefish
flamefish.description: A bright red cardinalfish with two white lines through the eye, a dark spot below the rear dorsal fin and a dark bar at the tail base.
flamefish.tip: Hides in holes by day and comes out at night. Point your light at the edge of its hole, not straight at it.

flamingo-tongue.name: Flamingo tongue
flamingo-tongue.description: A thumbnail snail wrapped in orange leopard print, grazing on sea fans.
flamingo-tongue.tip: Search the sea fans, not the coral. The pattern is living tissue, not the shell.

florida-horse-conch.name: Florida horse conch
florida-horse-conch.description: A huge, spindle-shaped shell up to 60 cm long, with a brick-orange animal inside, on sand and seagrass.
florida-horse-conch.tip: Watch it hunt other snails, and leave every live shell where it lies.

flying-gurnard.name: Flying gurnard
flying-gurnard.description: A bottom fish with a blunt, armored head and broad pectoral fins, spotted with blue, that fan open like wings when it is startled.
flying-gurnard.tip: Scan sand and rubble near the reef edge, where it walks along the bottom. Stay back; a close approach makes it flare its fins and flee.

foureye-butterflyfish.name: Foureye butterflyfish
foureye-butterflyfish.description: A pale disc with one big false eyespot near the tail, to send a predator the wrong way.
foureye-butterflyfish.tip: Approach from the side; head-on they turn and show you the fake eye.

french-angelfish.name: French angelfish
french-angelfish.description: A tall, dark disc scaled in tiny yellow crescents, usually in pairs.
french-angelfish.tip: Stay still for a moment beside a sponge and the pair often comes to look at you.

french-grunt.name: French grunt
french-grunt.description: Yellow-striped fish stacked in the hundreds around coral heads.
french-grunt.tip: Move slowly into the school and it will part and reform around you.

gag.name: Gag
gag.description: A long gray grouper marked with darker, worm-like blotches and dark-edged fins; old males darken almost to black.
gag.tip: Look on ledges and wrecks off Florida and in the Gulf of Mexico. Hold your position and a curious gag will often come in for a look.

garden-eel.name: Garden eel
garden-eel.description: A field of pencil-thin eels standing out of the sand, swaying into the current.
garden-eel.tip: They vanish as you approach. Settle at a distance, wait, and the whole field grows back.

giant-anemone.name: Giant Caribbean anemone
giant-anemone.description: A bouquet of purple- or pink-tipped tentacles, often with a shrimp living in it.
giant-anemone.tip: Look inside before you move on. The cleaner shrimp are the real find.

giant-barrel-sponge.name: Giant barrel sponge
giant-barrel-sponge.description: A rust-colored barrel wide enough to climb into, and centuries old.
giant-barrel-sponge.tip: Never rest a hand on the rim. Some of these were here before Florida was a state.

giant-basket-star.name: Giant basket star
giant-basket-star.description: A tangle of branching arms that opens into a feeding net after dark.
giant-basket-star.tip: By day it is a knot on a sea rod. Come back at night to see it open.

giant-hermit-crab.name: Giant hermit crab
giant-hermit-crab.description: A big red hermit with heavy, bumpy claws, living in a large conch shell on sand and seagrass.
giant-hermit-crab.tip: Watch for a big shell that moves on the sand, then settle and wait for the eyes to come out.

giant-manta-ray.name: Giant manta ray
giant-manta-ray.description: A very broad, dark-backed ray with a white belly, wide cephalic fins at the mouth and a pale shoulder patch.
giant-manta-ray.tip: Seen on Caribbean seamounts and cleaning stations, mostly in the cooler months. Keep your distance, never touch or chase it, and let it choose to circle.

glasseye-snapper.name: Glasseye snapper
glasseye-snapper.description: Red and silver with an enormous eye, hanging head-down in a shaded hollow.
glasseye-snapper.tip: A night feeder resting by day. Any dark recess at eye level is worth a second look.

glassy-sweeper.name: Glassy sweeper
glassy-sweeper.description: Copper-colored clouds that fill the shaded spaces inside a wreck or ledge.
glassy-sweeper.tip: Stay outside the structure and let the school reform around you.

golden-coral-shrimp.name: Golden coral shrimp
golden-coral-shrimp.description: A small golden-yellow shrimp with red-and-white banded claws and long white antennae, sheltering in a crevice.
golden-coral-shrimp.tip: Look deep under ledges near moray eels, which it often cleans, with a light and never a hand.

golden-crinoid.name: Golden crinoid
golden-crinoid.description: A feather star with orange-yellow, feathery arms, often with a dark line down each one, reaching out of a crevice.
golden-crinoid.tip: Keep your fins clear; the arms break off at the lightest touch.

goldentail-moray.name: Goldentail moray
goldentail-moray.description: Dark brown flecked with gold, small enough to live in a fist-sized hole.
goldentail-moray.tip: Scan holes at chest height on the reef face as well as at the base.

goldspot-goby.name: Goldspot goby
goldspot-goby.description: A speckled sand-colored goby with a dark bar down through the eye and a small gold spot above the pectoral fin.
goldspot-goby.tip: It rests on sand beside the reef and darts a short way when you come close. Stop a body length off and let it settle.

goldspotted-eel.name: Goldspotted eel
goldspotted-eel.description: A tan snake eel with a row of dark spots ringed in gold along each side, often seen with its head out of the sand or sliding across it.
goldspotted-eel.tip: Look over sand and rubble at dusk and on night dives. Keep your hands and fins off the bottom around it; it retreats into the sand if crowded.

goliath-grouper.name: Goliath grouper
goliath-grouper.description: Enormous and unbothered, usually parked under a ledge or in a wreck’s shadow.
goliath-grouper.tip: Give it room and never block its way out from under an overhang.

gray-angelfish.name: Gray angelfish
gray-angelfish.description: The French angelfish’s larger, plainer cousin, with a pale square-cut tail.
gray-angelfish.tip: Tell it from a French angelfish by the tail: square and light, not round and dark.

gray-snapper.name: Gray snapper
gray-snapper.description: Wary gray-red snapper that hang in the lee of wrecks and mangrove roots.
gray-snapper.tip: They watch you first. Approach at an angle rather than head-on and they hold.

gray-triggerfish.name: Gray triggerfish
gray-triggerfish.description: A plain gray to olive triggerfish with faint darker bars and fine blue specks, swimming by rippling its upper and lower fins.
gray-triggerfish.tip: Common on wrecks and rigs. Nesting fish guard the sand below, so give the nest a wide berth.

graysby.name: Graysby
graysby.description: A small pale grouper freckled all over, with four dots along the top of the back.
graysby.tip: Count the four dots on the dorsal ridge. That is the tell against every other small grouper.

great-barracuda.name: Great barracuda
great-barracuda.description: A long silver bar with an underslung jaw, hanging motionless in the current.
great-barracuda.tip: It is curious, not interested in you. Leave shiny gear tucked away and carry on.

great-hammerhead.name: Great hammerhead
great-hammerhead.description: A large, solitary shark with a tall first dorsal fin and a wide head with an almost straight front edge.
great-hammerhead.tip: Meet it on open-water edges and flats, mostly in winter. Keep your distance, don’t chase it, and let it pass.

great-star-coral.name: Great star coral
great-star-coral.description: Boulders studded with fat, evenly spaced cups that open and feed at night.
great-star-coral.tip: Come back with a light after dark. The whole boulder is in bloom.

greater-amberjack.name: Greater amberjack
greater-amberjack.description: A big, powerful jack with an amber stripe along the side and a dark diagonal band through the eye.
greater-amberjack.tip: Often circles divers on deep wrecks out of curiosity. Hold your position on the line and let them come to look.

greater-soapfish.name: Greater soapfish
greater-soapfish.description: A drab gray-brown fish with a pointed head and a scatter of small pale blotches, lying still at the base of coral or in a cave mouth.
greater-soapfish.tip: Easy to mistake for a resting grouper. Look along the bottom of ledges, and leave it alone: its skin slime is bitter and irritating.

green-clinging-crab.name: Green clinging crab
green-clinging-crab.description: A small, bright green crab with a lumpy shell and heavy green claws whose fingers are scooped and tipped in white, tucked into coral crevices.
green-clinging-crab.tip: Check the bases of anemones and the gaps in coral rubble, best at night. Light it from the side so it stays put.

green-finger-sponge.name: Green finger sponge
green-finger-sponge.description: Dark green to almost black branching fingers, often dotted with tiny yellow zoanthids.
green-finger-sponge.tip: It reads black until a light hits it. Use one to see the green, and the zoanthids spread over the branches.

green-moray.name: Green moray
green-moray.description: A heavy olive eel that fills a crevice and breathes with its mouth open.
green-moray.tip: The open mouth is breathing, not a threat. Keep hands away and it stays calm.

green-razorfish.name: Green razorfish
green-razorfish.description: A small, flat-sided wrasse with a steep blunt head, green to mottled, hovering over sand and seagrass. Males carry a dark spot mid-body.
green-razorfish.tip: Approach slowly over open sand. If it feels crowded it dives headfirst into the sand and stays there.

green-sea-turtle.name: Green sea turtle
green-sea-turtle.description: A smooth-shelled grazer, usually head-down in seagrass or asleep under a ledge.
green-sea-turtle.tip: Stay off its path to the surface. It has to breathe, and it will not go around you.

grooved-brain-coral.name: Grooved brain coral
grooved-brain-coral.description: A rounded head patterned with maze-like ridges and deep valleys.
grooved-brain-coral.tip: Notice the pattern while keeping fins and hands safely clear.

hairy-blenny.name: Hairy blenny
hairy-blenny.description: A big, mottled brown-green blenny with tufts of cirri over the eyes and a dark eyespot on the gill cover, in rocky shallows.
hairy-blenny.tip: Check holes and crevices in rocky shallows and jetties. It rests head-out and will hold still if you approach slowly.

hardhead-silverside.name: Hardhead silverside
hardhead-silverside.description: A small, slim fish with a bright silver stripe along each side, packed into dense schools.
hardhead-silverside.tip: Watch the school from outside the opening. They gather in overhead spaces, so stay out of caverns and swim-throughs.

harlequin-bass.name: Harlequin bass
harlequin-bass.description: A finger-length bass with a pointed snout, white with bold black bars and spots, perched on rubble near the reef.
harlequin-bass.tip: It stays put and lets you come close. Move in slowly at its level and it will often hold its ground.

hawksbill-turtle.name: Hawksbill turtle
hawksbill-turtle.description: A narrow beak and a serrated shell edge, picking sponges off the reef face.
hawksbill-turtle.tip: The beak is the tell: pointed and hooked, where a green turtle’s is blunt. Watch from the side and never touch or chase it.

highhat.name: Highhat
highhat.description: A dark drum with crisp white stripes and a tall first back fin; juveniles carry it as a long, curved banner.
highhat.tip: Check the shaded floor under ledges and in holes, where small groups circle the same spot all day.

hogfish.name: Hogfish
hogfish.description: A long-snouted wrasse that roots through sand and rubble for shellfish.
hogfish.tip: Follow the puffs of sand. It makes the mess before you spot the fish.

honeycomb-cowfish.name: Honeycomb cowfish
honeycomb-cowfish.description: A boxy fish tiled in hexagons, with two small horns over the eyes.
honeycomb-cowfish.tip: Look low over the sand between coral heads; it hovers rather than swims.

horse-eye-jack.name: Horse-eye jack
horse-eye-jack.description: Big-eyed silver jacks that roll past in tight, fast schools.
horse-eye-jack.tip: Watch the blue over the wreck for a wall of them rather than scanning the deck.

hovering-dartfish.name: Hovering dartfish
hovering-dartfish.description: A slender pale-blue fish with neon lines on the face, hanging a hand’s width above its burrow in sand or rubble.
hovering-dartfish.tip: It vanishes into the hole at the first fast move. Come in low and slow, and stop well short.

humpback-whale.name: Humpback whale
humpback-whale.description: A huge whale with long white flippers, a knobby head and a black-and-white tail it lifts before a dive.
humpback-whale.tip: Follow local rules and the crew’s lead: keep your distance, slip in without splashing, and let the whale set the pace.

indigo-hamlet.name: Indigo hamlet
indigo-hamlet.description: Deep blue banded with white, and one of the harder Caribbean fish to find.
indigo-hamlet.tip: Worth the whole dive if you get one. Try the deeper coral heads, not the shallows.

jackknife-fish.name: Jackknife-fish
jackknife-fish.description: A black-and-white fish with a tall, curved dorsal fin like an open blade, and a long dark stripe along the body. Juveniles trail a streaming dorsal fin.
jackknife-fish.tip: Look under ledges and in caves and crevices, often in a pair. It hangs in shadow, so approach slowly and let it settle.

knobby-brain-coral.name: Knobby brain coral
knobby-brain-coral.description: Low crusts and mounds raised into lumpy knobs, covered in short, narrow winding valleys.
knobby-brain-coral.tip: Mostly a shallow back-reef coral. The knobs are what tell it apart from the smoother symmetrical brain coral.

lamarcks-sheet-coral.name: Lamarck’s sheet coral
lamarcks-sheet-coral.description: Broad plates stacked down a wall, with curving ridges and small white star-shaped polyps scattered across the surface.
lamarcks-sheet-coral.tip: A wall coral, mostly below 15 meters. Hold your depth off the plates; they snap under a fin.

lancer-dragonet.name: Lancer dragonet
lancer-dragonet.description: A small, flat-headed fish, mottled brown and gray to blend with the bottom, with a tall, striped dorsal fin it raises to display, resting on sand and rubble.
lancer-dragonet.tip: Scan open sand near the reef, especially in shallow water. It sits so still it is easy to miss, so look for the fin and the eyes.

lane-snapper.name: Lane snapper
lane-snapper.description: A small pinkish snapper with gold lines along the sides and a dark spot high on the flank below the back fin.
lane-snapper.tip: Look over seagrass and sand beside the reef, where small groups cruise close over the bottom.

lantern-bass.name: Lantern bass
lantern-bass.description: A thumb-sized sea bass, pale with orange-red patches and a row of four dark squarish spots along the lower side.
lantern-bass.tip: Sweep rubble and the edges of seagrass in shallow water. It perches on the bottom and holds still if you do.

lavender-rope-sponge.name: Lavender rope sponge
lavender-rope-sponge.description: Lavender to blue-gray ropes with a rough, finely bumpy skin, upright or trailing over the reef.
lavender-rope-sponge.tip: Look closely along the ropes: small brittle stars wrap their arms around them and come out to feed at night.

leatherback-sea-turtle.name: Leatherback sea turtle
leatherback-sea-turtle.description: The largest turtle, up to two meters, with a dark, leathery shell ridged lengthwise and flecked white, usually met in open water.
leatherback-sea-turtle.tip: Protected: give it room, never chase or touch it, and let it choose the distance.

lemon-shark.name: Lemon shark
lemon-shark.description: Yellow-brown, blunt-nosed, with two dorsal fins nearly the same size.
lemon-shark.tip: Common over sand flats and in shallow channels, so look away from the coral.

lesser-starlet-coral.name: Lesser starlet coral
lesser-starlet-coral.description: Small crusts and fist-sized lumps with deep, crisp cups, scattered over sand, rubble and seagrass in shallow water.
lesser-starlet-coral.tip: Easy to miss on a shallow entry. Look at your feet in the first few meters, and keep them off the bottom.

lettuce-coral.name: Lettuce coral
lettuce-coral.description: Thin ruffled plates growing in overlapping layers down the shaded side of a slope.
lettuce-coral.tip: Grows where the light is poor, so look under and behind rather than on top.

lettuce-sea-slug.name: Lettuce sea slug
lettuce-sea-slug.description: Ruffled green frills on a slug the size of a coin, grazing on rock and rubble.
lettuce-sea-slug.tip: It keeps the algae’s chloroplasts alive inside itself and feeds on sunlight. Look in the shallows.

lionfish.name: Lionfish
lionfish.description: Striped fans of venomous spines, beautiful and not from this ocean.
lionfish.tip: Invasive here. Admire it, keep well clear of the spines, and report it to the crew.

loggerhead-turtle.name: Loggerhead turtle
loggerhead-turtle.description: A heavy reddish head built for crushing conch and lobster.
loggerhead-turtle.tip: Give a feeding loggerhead a wide berth. That jaw is doing serious work.

long-spined-urchin.name: Long-spined sea urchin
long-spined-urchin.description: A black pincushion with spines as long as your hand; the reef’s best grazer.
long-spined-urchin.tip: Mind your knees and fins in a swim-through. The spines break off in you.

longfin-damselfish.name: Longfin damselfish
longfin-damselfish.description: Juveniles are bright yellow with blue lines on the head and back and a black spot on the back fin; adults turn dark brown with long, trailing fin tips.
longfin-damselfish.tip: The yellow young hide among coral rubble and branching coral. Stay still and they will reappear from the same crack.

longjaw-squirrelfish.name: Longjaw squirrelfish
longjaw-squirrelfish.description: A red-orange squirrelfish lined in gold, with a yellow-orange spiny back fin and a lower jaw that juts past the upper.
longjaw-squirrelfish.tip: Look under ledges and into cracks on deeper reef by day. A light brings out the gold stripes.

longlure-frogfish.name: Longlure frogfish
longlure-frogfish.description: A lumpy sponge that turns out to have a mouth, fishing with a lure on its head.
longlure-frogfish.tip: Guides find these and divers do not. If your guide stops at bare sponge, look harder.

longnose-batfish.name: Longnose batfish
longnose-batfish.description: A flattened, warty, orange-brown fish with a short horn on its snout, red lips and arm-like pectoral fins, that walks on the bottom instead of swimming.
longnose-batfish.tip: Look on sand and rubble and on night dives, where it looks like a bit of debris until it moves. Watch from a distance; it will not swim off, but it is not a fish to poke.

longsnout-butterflyfish.name: Longsnout butterflyfish
longsnout-butterflyfish.description: Small, yellow-backed and long-faced, working the shaded parts of a wall.
longsnout-butterflyfish.tip: A wall fish rather than a reef-flat one, so look under overhangs on the way back up.

longsnout-seahorse.name: Longsnout seahorse
longsnout-seahorse.description: A seahorse the length of a finger, anchored by its tail to a sponge or a rope.
longsnout-seahorse.tip: Never move one for a photograph, and keep the light off it, because bright light stresses them.

longspine-squirrelfish.name: Longspine squirrelfish
longspine-squirrelfish.description: A red and silver squirrelfish with a white triangle at the tip of each dorsal spine and a long upper tail lobe.
longspine-squirrelfish.tip: The white-tipped back fin is what sets it apart from the common squirrelfish. Look in cracks and under ledges by day.

lumpy-overgrowing-sponge.name: Lumpy overgrowing sponge
lumpy-overgrowing-sponge.description: A soft pink to lavender mass of lumps riddled with holes, spreading over sea rods, sponges and rock.
lumpy-overgrowing-sponge.tip: Follow a sea rod down to its base. This sponge often swallows the lower branches whole.

mahogany-snapper.name: Mahogany snapper
mahogany-snapper.description: Silver with red-edged fins and a big eye, in loose crowds over the coral by day.
mahogany-snapper.tip: Drifts rather than schools tightly. Move through the group slowly and it barely reacts.

manatee.name: West Indian manatee
manatee.description: A gray, slow, whiskered grazer of warm springs and inshore channels.
manatee.tip: Protected: passive observation only. Hands off, no pursuit, no blocking its route.

masked-goby.name: Masked goby
masked-goby.description: A tiny see-through amber goby with white dashes down the back and a dark band across the eyes, hovering in loose swarms.
masked-goby.tip: Shine a light under ledges and into cave mouths. Dozens may hang there, each a few centimeters long.

masked-hamlet.name: Masked hamlet
masked-hamlet.description: A pale gray to white hamlet with a black mask through the eye and onto the snout, a dark tail and bright blue pelvic fins.
masked-hamlet.tip: A western Caribbean fish, common in Cayman. Look along the reef base and let it settle before you move in.

massive-starlet-coral.name: Massive starlet coral
massive-starlet-coral.description: Smooth rounded domes in tan, brown or rust, the surface packed with small, even pinhole cups.
massive-starlet-coral.tip: Bring your eye close: each pinhole is a tiny star-shaped cup. Look, but keep hands and fins off the dome.

maze-coral.name: Maze coral
maze-coral.description: Wide, deep valleys running in long curves, like a brain coral drawn with a bigger pen.
maze-coral.tip: Tell it from a brain coral by the valleys: fewer, wider, and running further before they turn.

midnight-parrotfish.name: Midnight parrotfish
midnight-parrotfish.description: Deep blue-black all over, with a brighter blue beak; big and easy to miss.
midnight-parrotfish.tip: It reads as a dark shape against dark coral. Look for the beak, not the body.

moon-jelly.name: Moon jelly
moon-jelly.description: A translucent saucer with four horseshoe rings, pulsing through open water.
moon-jelly.tip: Mild sting at worst, but a hood and a full suit make a swarm a pleasure instead of a chore.

mountainous-star-coral.name: Mountainous star coral
mountainous-star-coral.description: Great mounded sheets with a fine even texture, the biggest heads on many reefs.
mountainous-star-coral.tip: Pale patches are bleaching, not a pattern. Worth reporting to the crew if you see a lot.

mustard-hill-coral.name: Mustard hill coral
mustard-hill-coral.description: Low mustard-yellow domes with a bumpy surface, common in the shallows.
mustard-hill-coral.tip: One of the few corals doing well right now. You will see it on almost every dive.

mutton-snapper.name: Mutton snapper
mutton-snapper.description: Olive above and rose below, with a small black spot high on the flank.
mutton-snapper.tip: Hunts over sand at the reef edge, so look away from the coral rather than into it.

nassau-grouper.name: Nassau grouper
nassau-grouper.description: Banded brown and cream with a dark saddle at the tail, and famously curious.
nassau-grouper.tip: Protected and slow to recover. Look, photograph, and leave it where it is.

neon-goby.name: Neon goby
neon-goby.description: A finger-length black goby with a bright blue stripe from eye to tail, the cleaner of Florida and Gulf of Mexico reefs.
neon-goby.tip: Groupers and morays open their mouths and let it in. Watch the station from a short way off so the customers stay.

netted-barrel-sponge.name: Netted barrel sponge
netted-barrel-sponge.description: A large barrel or bowl, yellow-green to brown, the outside covered in deep pits divided by a net of ridges.
netted-barrel-sponge.tip: Run your eye over the outer wall: the netted pits set it apart from the smoother giant barrel sponge.

night-sergeant.name: Night sergeant
night-sergeant.description: A stocky damselfish with five broad dark bars on a tan to olive body and no yellow, living in the surge along rocky shores.
night-sergeant.tip: Look in the first few meters off a rocky entry, where the swell breaks. Hold onto nothing and let the surge carry you past.

nimble-spray-crab.name: Nimble spray crab
nimble-spray-crab.description: A flat, spidery crab with long legs ringed in gold, clinging to rock in the shallow surge.
nimble-spray-crab.tip: Check under long-spined urchins and rock ledges in the shallows with a light, not a hand; it darts sideways at the slightest move.

nurse-shark.name: Nurse shark
nurse-shark.description: A broad, mellow bottom-rester with rounded fins and two barbels at the snout.
nurse-shark.tip: Check quiet ledges without crowding or blocking an animal’s way out. Never touch or grab one; it bites when handled.

ocean-surgeonfish.name: Ocean surgeonfish
ocean-surgeonfish.description: Plain blue-gray to brown with no body bars and a deep crescent tail with long tips, grazing in roving groups.
ocean-surgeonfish.tip: No bars and a sickle tail mean ocean surgeonfish. Give the group room and it will graze past you.

ocean-triggerfish.name: Ocean triggerfish
ocean-triggerfish.description: A tall gray diamond with a dark blotch at the pectoral, out in the blue off a wall.
ocean-triggerfish.tip: Look off the wall rather than along it. This one hangs in open water, not on the reef.

oceanic-whitetip-shark.name: Oceanic whitetip shark
oceanic-whitetip-shark.description: A slow, stocky open-ocean shark with long rounded fins tipped in white and a blunt snout.
oceanic-whitetip-shark.tip: Keep it in view, stay close to the group and the line, don’t turn your back, and end the dive if it stays. Never leave the line to follow it.

orange-cup-coral.name: Orange cup coral
orange-cup-coral.description: Clusters of round orange to reddish cups in shade under ledges, in caves and on wrecks and rigs, opening bright yellow-orange tentacles after dark. An Indo-Pacific coral, not from this ocean.
orange-cup-coral.tip: Invasive here. Come back on a night dive to see the tentacles open.

orange-elephant-ear-sponge.name: Orange elephant ear sponge
orange-elephant-ear-sponge.description: Broad orange sheets folded out from a wall, the brightest thing at depth.
orange-elephant-ear-sponge.tip: Hawksbill turtles eat these. A chewed edge means one has been through recently.

orangeclaw-hermit-crab.name: Orangeclaw hermit crab
orangeclaw-hermit-crab.description: A small hermit with bright orange claws and red-brown, white-tipped legs, in a borrowed snail shell.
orangeclaw-hermit-crab.tip: Watch shallow rubble and rock in calm water; it wanders in the open by day.

orangesided-goby.name: Orangesided goby
orangesided-goby.description: A tiny goby with a pale body crossed by red-orange blotches along the side and a bright, speckled red-orange head, perched on corals and sponges.
orangesided-goby.tip: Look low on coral heads and sponges in shallow reef, and watch for the orange flash. It is small and shy, so settle in a hand’s width away and keep still.

orangespotted-filefish.name: Orangespotted filefish
orangespotted-filefish.description: A small brown filefish dotted with tiny orange spots, with pale lines along the body and a white spot above and below the tail base.
orangespotted-filefish.tip: Shy and quick to slip behind coral. Watch from a little way off and it may keep picking at the reef in view.

pallid-goby.name: Pallid goby
pallid-goby.description: A pale, almost see-through goby with a short yellow line edged in dark running back from the eye, resting on sand beside coral.
pallid-goby.tip: Look on the sand patches right against coral heads. It sits still on its fins and dashes a short way if you crowd it.

peacock-flounder.name: Peacock flounder
peacock-flounder.description: A flat sand-colored disc with blue rings, both eyes on one side.
peacock-flounder.tip: It only becomes visible when it moves, so sweep the sand rather than staring at it.

pederson-cleaner-shrimp.name: Pederson cleaner shrimp
pederson-cleaner-shrimp.description: A glass shrimp with violet spots, waving from inside an anemone.
pederson-cleaner-shrimp.tip: Settle a hand’s length from the anemone and hold still. It comes to the edge and works whatever fish stops there.

peppermint-goby.name: Peppermint goby
peppermint-goby.description: A tiny see-through goby washed in orange and yellow, with a dark blue snout and eyes, perched on the top of living coral.
peppermint-goby.tip: Scan the upper surface of star and brain corals. It sits still on the polyps, so a slow, close look finds it.

permit-fish.name: Permit
permit-fish.description: A tall, mirror-flat silver disc that appears over wrecks and vanishes as fast.
permit-fish.tip: Keep the camera ready on the descent. Permit meet you on the way down, not at depth.

pillar-coral.name: Pillar coral
pillar-coral.description: Furry-looking spires standing upright off the bottom; rare and getting rarer.
pillar-coral.tip: The fuzz is polyps out feeding by day, and few corals do that.

pink-meanie.name: Pink meanie
pink-meanie.description: A pinkish bell trailing long, fine tentacles, often tangled around the moon jellies it eats.
pink-meanie.tip: The tentacles reach far past the bell, so give it a wide berth and watch from the side.

pink-vase-sponge.name: Pink vase sponge
pink-vase-sponge.description: A pink to lavender vase with a rough, fuzzy wall and a ragged rim fringed with small fingers.
pink-vase-sponge.tip: The color fades to gray without a light at depth. Shine one across it from the side to bring the pink back.

pitted-sponge.name: Pitted sponge
pitted-sponge.description: Yellow to olive tubes and mounds whose surface is dimpled all over with deep, even pits like a honeycomb.
pitted-sponge.tip: Where it is broken it turns purple-black within minutes. A dark scar on one means a fin got there first.

porcupinefish.name: Porcupinefish
porcupinefish.description: A big-eyed spiny balloon that wedges itself under a ledge to sleep.
porcupinefish.tip: Never provoke one into inflating. It is a stress response, not a trick.

porkfish.name: Porkfish
porkfish.description: Two black head bars and a yellow body, the tidiest fish on the reef.
porkfish.tip: Check the up-current side of a coral head, where they hold station together.

portuguese-man-o-war.name: Portuguese man o’ war
portuguese-man-o-war.description: A blue to violet gas float with a pink crest, trailing long blue tentacles under the surface.
portuguese-man-o-war.tip: Keep well clear at the surface and on ascent; the tentacles hang meters down and sting even when broken off.

princess-parrotfish.name: Princess parrotfish
princess-parrotfish.description: Blue-green with two bright stripes along the face, grazing in small groups.
princess-parrotfish.tip: The stripes run through the eye, which is what separates it from a striped parrotfish.

puddingwife.name: Puddingwife
puddingwife.description: A large wrasse in blue-green and gold, with blue lines across the face and a dark spot at the base of the pectoral fin.
puddingwife.tip: It keeps its distance and swims a wide circle. Stay put on the edge of a sand patch and it may swing back in.

purple-reeffish.name: Purple reeffish
purple-reeffish.description: A small, deep blue-purple chromis; the young are a brighter electric blue.
purple-reeffish.tip: Found on deeper reef slopes near the bottom. Slow down at depth and look for the blue flicker in holes.

queen-angelfish.name: Queen angelfish
queen-angelfish.description: Blue and gold with a ringed crown on the forehead and long trailing fins.
queen-angelfish.tip: Quiet breathing helps: it keeps a coral head between you and it if you rush.

queen-conch.name: Queen conch
queen-conch.description: A heavy flared shell on seagrass sand, dragging itself along on one foot.
queen-conch.tip: Protected in Florida. Look for the two stalked eyes, and put nothing in your pocket.

queen-parrotfish.name: Queen parrotfish
queen-parrotfish.description: Blue-green with bright bands running from the beak, grazing along the coral.
queen-parrotfish.tip: Follow the crunching sound; you will hear it working before you see it.

queen-triggerfish.name: Queen triggerfish
queen-triggerfish.description: Blue-lined and gaudy, swimming with a rippling pair of fins rather than its tail.
queen-triggerfish.tip: Nesting fish defend a cone of water above the nest, so go around, not over.

ragged-sea-hare.name: Ragged sea hare
ragged-sea-hare.description: A shaggy, brown-gray sea hare covered in branching skin tassels and tiny blue spots, on sand and mud.
ragged-sea-hare.tip: Look in calm, shallow lagoons and along seagrass edges, and leave it on the bottom where you found it.

rainbow-parrotfish.name: Rainbow parrotfish
rainbow-parrotfish.description: The biggest parrotfish in the Atlantic: bronze-green, and over a meter grown.
rainbow-parrotfish.tip: It grows up in the mangroves, so a reef beside one is where you have the best chance.

rainbow-runner.name: Rainbow runner
rainbow-runner.description: A sleek, olive-blue fish with two pale blue stripes edged in yellow along the flank, and a deeply forked tail.
rainbow-runner.tip: Watch the blue water near walls and offshore pinnacles, often in small groups. They pass in a hurry, so hold your position and let them come.

red-boring-sponge.name: Red boring sponge
red-boring-sponge.description: Bright red-orange patches set into coral heads, with raised round openings, eating into the coral from inside.
red-boring-sponge.tip: Look on star and brain corals for red patches edged in white dead skeleton. It thrives where the water is polluted.

red-grouper.name: Red grouper
red-grouper.description: Rust-colored, square-jawed, and dug into its own excavated hollow in the bottom.
red-grouper.tip: Look for a scooped pit in the sand or rubble. The fish is usually sitting in it.

red-hind.name: Red hind
red-hind.description: A pale grouper covered in small red spots, with the soft fins and tail edged in black.
red-hind.tip: Rests on the bottom near coral and rubble. The black fin edges tell it from the rock hind.

red-reef-hermit.name: Red reef hermit
red-reef-hermit.description: A scarlet hermit with yellow eyestalks and bristly legs, tucked into an old shell in a reef crevice.
red-reef-hermit.tip: Peer into small holes in the reef; under a light the red legs stand out at once.

red-rope-sponge.name: Erect rope sponge
red-rope-sponge.description: Deep red cords standing off the reef, stiff and slightly branched.
red-rope-sponge.tip: The red survives deeper than most colors, which makes it a useful marker on a wall.

redband-parrotfish.name: Redband parrotfish
redband-parrotfish.description: Small and mottled, with a pale patch behind the head and a red-edged tail.
redband-parrotfish.tip: The commonest parrotfish on most Caribbean reefs, and the one nobody stops to look at.

redlip-blenny.name: Redlip blenny
redlip-blenny.description: A dark, blunt-headed little fish propped on its fins in a hole in the coral.
redlip-blenny.tip: Shallow and territorial. Check the same knob of coral twice and it will be back out.

redspotted-hawkfish.name: Redspotted hawkfish
redspotted-hawkfish.description: A small perching fish with dark bars, red freckles on the head and back, and tufts on the tips of its dorsal spines.
redspotted-hawkfish.tip: It sits on coral and sponges on its stiff lower fins. Come in slowly from the side and it often stays put for a long look.

redtail-parrotfish.name: Redtail parrotfish
redtail-parrotfish.description: Terminal males are blue-green with a dark spot at the pectoral base and a red-orange patch in the tail; younger fish are mottled reddish brown.
redtail-parrotfish.tip: Often grazes near seagrass and patch reefs. Females can switch color in seconds to blend with the bottom, so watch the ones that seem to vanish.

reef-butterflyfish.name: Reef butterflyfish
reef-butterflyfish.description: Pale with a dark wash across the back half, always somewhere near its partner.
reef-butterflyfish.tip: Deeper than the other butterflyfish here. Expect it below twenty meters, in pairs.

reef-urchin.name: Reef urchin
reef-urchin.description: A small urchin with long greenish to olive spines, each with a pale ring at the base and a dark, often violet tip, set on a reddish-brown body.
reef-urchin.tip: Shine a light into shallow crevices and under ledges, where it hides by day; at night it creeps out to graze, so keep hands and knees clear.

remora.name: Remora
remora.description: A striped rider that detaches from its host and circles whatever comes past.
remora.tip: If one takes an interest in you, keep swimming and it loses interest.

rock-beauty.name: Rock beauty
rock-beauty.description: Yellow at both ends with a black saddle in the middle, never far from a hole.
rock-beauty.tip: Watch one gap in the reef rather than sweeping. It comes back out to the same spot.

rock-boring-urchin.name: Rock-boring urchin
rock-boring-urchin.description: A stout urchin with short black to reddish spines, wedged into a hole it has ground into shallow rock.
rock-boring-urchin.tip: Watch your hands and knees in the surge zone; it lines shoreline rock by the hundreds.

rock-hind.name: Rock hind
rock-hind.description: A stocky grouper covered in red-brown spots, wedged into rubble or a wreck plate.
rock-hind.tip: Prefers broken ground to clean coral. Search the rubble field, not the reef top.

rose-coral.name: Rose coral
rose-coral.description: A palm-sized oval coral folded into deep winding valleys like a rose, lying loose on sand or in seagrass.
rose-coral.tip: Search seagrass beds and sandy patches near the reef. Leave it where it lies; never turn it over.

rosy-razorfish.name: Rosy razorfish
rosy-razorfish.description: A small, flat-sided wrasse with a steep blunt head, pale green-gray fading to pink below, living in colonies over open sand.
rosy-razorfish.tip: Come in slowly and low. When one feels crowded it dives into the sand, and the rest of the colony follows.

roughhead-blenny.name: Roughhead blenny
roughhead-blenny.description: A tiny blenny that lives in an old worm hole in coral, showing only its head, crowned with branched tufts.
roughhead-blenny.tip: Scan the dead tops of coral heads for holes the size of a pencil, then hold still. Shadows send it back inside.

roughtail-stingray.name: Roughtail stingray
roughtail-stingray.description: A very large, dark gray-brown diamond with a long tail that is rough with small thorns, gliding or resting on sand in cooler or deeper water.
roughtail-stingray.tip: Look along sand edges and channels deeper than the usual ray dive. Give it a wide berth and watch from the side, never from above or behind the tail.

round-scad.name: Round scad
round-scad.description: A slim, silvery baitfish with a row of small dark spots along the lateral line, moving in tight, fast schools.
round-scad.tip: Watch for a shimmering ball in midwater above the reef. Jacks and mackerel are usually close behind.

row-pore-rope-sponge.name: Row pore rope sponge
row-pore-rope-sponge.description: Long thin lavender to reddish ropes sprawled across the reef, with small pores set in neat lines along each rope.
row-pore-rope-sponge.tip: Get close to see the pores running in rows. That line is what tells it from the other rope sponges.

royal-gramma.name: Royal gramma
royal-gramma.description: Purple in front, gold behind, thumb-sized, and often swimming upside down.
royal-gramma.tip: Look into the roof of a small cave or under a ledge. It orients its belly to the rock.

saddled-blenny.name: Saddled blenny
saddled-blenny.description: A pale little blenny with four or five dark triangles down its side, their points aimed at the belly, perched on coral rubble.
saddled-blenny.tip: Common on shallow reef tops. Move slowly and it hops a short way to a new perch instead of vanishing.

sailfin-blenny.name: Sailfin blenny
sailfin-blenny.description: A tiny blenny living in a hole in rubble or sand. Males are dark, with a tall sail of a dorsal fin they flick up to display.
sailfin-blenny.tip: Lie off the sand flat and watch the holes. A male will pop up, raise his sail and drop back in.

sailors-choice.name: Sailor’s choice
sailors-choice.description: A silvery gray grunt covered in small dark spots that line up in slanting rows, with dusky fins.
sailors-choice.tip: Look in shallow seagrass and around rocky shores, where it mixes into schools with other grunts.

sand-diver.name: Sand diver
sand-diver.description: A propped-up lizardfish that sits on the sand until something small swims by.
sand-diver.tip: Look for a stick shape with eyes at the edge of a sand channel.

sand-perch.name: Sand perch
sand-perch.description: A slim sea bass of sand and seagrass, with brown bars down the body and blue and orange lines along the head.
sand-perch.tip: Look on open sand and rubble near the reef. It rests on the bottom and flicks off a short way when you get close.

sand-tilefish.name: Sand tilefish
sand-tilefish.description: A long, pale blue-white fish with a yellow-edged crescent tail, hovering over a rubble mound on open sand.
sand-tilefish.tip: Find the mound of coral bits on the sand. Stay back a few meters or it dives head-first into its burrow.

sargassum-triggerfish.name: Sargassum triggerfish
sargassum-triggerfish.description: A bluish-gray triggerfish with rows of dark spots along the side and three dark grooves on the cheek, usually on deep walls.
sargassum-triggerfish.tip: Look out into the blue from deep walls. The young drift with rafts of sargassum weed at the surface.

saucereye-porgy.name: Saucereye porgy
saucereye-porgy.description: A tall, silvery porgy with a steep forehead, a large eye and a short blue line under it, cruising alone near the reef.
saucereye-porgy.tip: Watch the sand edge of the reef. It picks along the bottom for crabs and shells and keeps a steady distance from divers.

scalloped-hammerhead.name: Scalloped hammerhead
scalloped-hammerhead.description: A gray-brown shark with a wide, flat head whose front edge is notched in the middle. Rare in the Caribbean.
scalloped-hammerhead.tip: If you see one, hold your position, breathe slowly and let it pass.

scamp.name: Scamp
scamp.description: A tan to brown grouper peppered with small dark spots in clusters, yellow at the corners of the mouth, with ragged tips on the tail.
scamp.tip: Found on ledges and wrecks from the Carolinas to the Gulf of Mexico. The broom-like tail edge tells it from other groupers.

scattered-pore-rope-sponge.name: Scattered pore rope sponge
scattered-pore-rope-sponge.description: Yellow to orange-brown ropes and fingers, with pores dotted over them at random rather than in rows.
scattered-pore-rope-sponge.tip: Compare a branch with any lavender rope sponge nearby; the color and the scattered pores make the call.

schoolmaster-snapper.name: Schoolmaster snapper
schoolmaster-snapper.description: Yellow-finned snapper that hover in the shade of coral heads and wreck plates.
schoolmaster-snapper.tip: Look into the structure rather than over it; they hold just inside the shadow line.

scrawled-cowfish.name: Scrawled cowfish
scrawled-cowfish.description: A boxy cowfish with two horns over the eyes, its body scribbled with blue lines and spots on a yellow to tan base.
scrawled-cowfish.tip: Look over seagrass and sand near the reef. It hovers slowly, so keep your distance and let it go about its business.

scrawled-filefish.name: Scrawled filefish
scrawled-filefish.description: Olive with blue scribbles, drifting nose-down like a leaf in the current.
scrawled-filefish.tip: It hides by going vertical, so check anything that looks like a piece of debris.

sea-plume.name: Sea plume
sea-plume.description: Feathery gorgonians that sway the whole reef in time with the swell.
sea-plume.tip: Watch them to read the surge before you commit to a swim-through.

sea-walnut.name: Sea walnut
sea-walnut.description: A clear, walnut-sized comb jelly with two large lobes and rows of combs that flash rainbow colors.
sea-walnut.tip: It can’t sting. Hang still in the water and watch the colors ripple down its rows.

seaweed-blenny.name: Seaweed blenny
seaweed-blenny.description: A small mottled blenny with a branched tuft over each eye and fine blue lines fanning from the eye, propped on its fins in algae and rock.
seaweed-blenny.tip: Check algae-covered rock, ledges and pilings in the shallows. It sits in the open and watches you, so come in low and slow.

sergeant-major.name: Sergeant major
sergeant-major.description: Small, striped and everywhere, guarding purple egg patches on hard surfaces.
sergeant-major.tip: A guarding male will bump your mask. Back off rather than push in.

sharknose-goby.name: Sharknose goby
sharknose-goby.description: A tiny neon-striped goby that runs a cleaning station on top of a coral head.
sharknose-goby.tip: Find one and wait. Whatever queues up for its service is the rest of the reef arriving.

sharpnose-puffer.name: Sharpnose puffer
sharpnose-puffer.description: A thumb-sized puffer with blue-lined eyes, hovering nose-down over the coral.
sharpnose-puffer.tip: Everywhere once you know it, and the easiest small fish on the reef to get close to.

sharptail-eel.name: Sharptail eel
sharptail-eel.description: A pale spotted eel out in the open over sand and seagrass, nosing under rubble.
sharptail-eel.tip: Unlike a moray it travels in daylight. A moving eel in the open is almost always this.

sheepshead.name: Sheepshead
sheepshead.description: A silver-gray porgy with five or six bold black bars and a mouth of human-looking teeth, around pilings, jetties and wrecks.
sheepshead.tip: Check the barnacle-covered legs of piers and bridges, where it crunches crabs and shellfish off the posts.

shortstripe-goby.name: Shortstripe goby
shortstripe-goby.description: A small gray goby with a short yellow stripe that starts at the snout and stops behind the eye, living inside tube and barrel sponges.
shortstripe-goby.tip: Look into the throat of a sponge from a hand’s length away. It sits on the inner wall and backs deeper if your shadow falls over the opening.

shy-hamlet.name: Shy hamlet
shy-hamlet.description: Bright yellow with a dark blue-black patch across the upper back, and blue-edged black marks around the eye and snout.
shy-hamlet.tip: True to the name it ducks into the coral when you close in. Stop a body length off and it comes back out.

silky-shark.name: Silky shark
silky-shark.description: A sleek, open-ocean shark, dark bronze-gray above and pale below, with a small ridge along the back and long, curved pectoral fins with dark tips.
silky-shark.tip: Mostly a blue-water species, met off steep walls and on drifting-rope or bluewater dives. On a provisioned dive, follow the crew’s briefing to the letter; anywhere else, treat it as an unplanned encounter: stay calm, keep it in view and end the dive.

silver-porgy.name: Silver porgy
silver-porgy.description: A deep-bodied silver porgy with a bold black saddle on the base of the tail, in small groups over rocky shallows.
silver-porgy.tip: Common along rocky shores and jetties. Hang still at the edge of the rocks and the group will come back to graze.

slate-pencil-urchin.name: Slate pencil urchin
slate-pencil-urchin.description: A small urchin with a few thick, blunt spines like pencil stubs, often crusted with algae and sponge.
slate-pencil-urchin.tip: Look in crevices and under rubble at night, when it comes out to graze.

slipper-lobster.name: Slipper lobster
slipper-lobster.description: A flattened, plate-like lobster with shovels for antennae, pressed into a crevice.
slipper-lobster.tip: It reads as a piece of the reef until it moves. Check the roof of a cave, not the floor.

slippery-dick.name: Slippery dick
slippery-dick.description: A pale greenish wrasse with a dark stripe from snout to tail, cruising low over sand, seagrass and rubble.
slippery-dick.tip: One of the most common wrasses in the shallows. Settle near a sand patch and it will work right past your fins.

smallmouth-grunt.name: Smallmouth grunt
smallmouth-grunt.description: Silvery white with even yellow stripes, yellow fins and a small mouth, packed in schools under ledges.
smallmouth-grunt.tip: Look under overhangs on shallow reefs by day. Stay low and outside the ledge so the school keeps its place.

smooth-flower-coral.name: Smooth flower coral
smooth-flower-coral.description: A small bush of short branches, each ending in a single smooth-walled oval cup the size of a coin.
smooth-flower-coral.tip: By day the cups look bare. Come back at night with a light and see the tentacles open.

smooth-trunkfish.name: Smooth trunkfish
smooth-trunkfish.description: A hovering box with pursed lips that blows sand away to find its food.
smooth-trunkfish.tip: Watch it puff at the sand. The whole feeding trick happens in a few seconds.

social-feather-duster.name: Social feather duster
social-feather-duster.description: Clusters of small feather dusters, each crown a soft brown, purple or white fan, crowded together on reef rock.
