social-feather-duster.tip: Hang still beside a cluster; if they pull in, wait and they reopen one by one.

southern-sennet.name: Southern sennet
southern-sennet.description: A slim, silver barracuda, much smaller than the great barracuda, with a long jaw and a faint dark bar or two on the upper flank, hanging in loose schools.
southern-sennet.tip: Look for schools hanging in the water over sand flats, grass and shallow reef. They drift away together if you swim straight at them, so approach slowly.

southern-stingray.name: Southern stingray
southern-stingray.description: A gray diamond gliding over the sand, or buried with only its eyes showing.
southern-stingray.tip: Give rays space and watch from the side, not from above.

spanish-grunt.name: Spanish grunt
spanish-grunt.description: A silver-gray grunt with bold dark stripes on the upper half, a yellow patch on the back near the tail and yellow-edged fins.
spanish-grunt.tip: Look under ledges on clear-water reefs, where it hangs with other grunts by day. Approach low and it holds its place.

spanish-hogfish.name: Spanish hogfish
spanish-hogfish.description: Purple over gold; the young ones run cleaning stations for bigger fish.
spanish-hogfish.tip: Find a juvenile at work and you have found the reef’s cleaning station.

spanish-lobster.name: Spanish lobster
spanish-lobster.description: A broad slipper lobster with shovel-plate antennae, a mottled tan shell and dark ringed spots near the tail.
spanish-lobster.tip: Look under ledges at night, when it walks out to hunt snails and clams.

spiny-lobster.name: Caribbean spiny lobster
spiny-lobster.description: No claws, but two long whips of antennae sticking out from under a ledge.
spiny-lobster.tip: The antennae give it away long before the body does. Check every dark gap.

spinyhead-blenny.name: Spinyhead blenny
spinyhead-blenny.description: A thumbnail-sized blenny peering out of an old worm hole in hard coral, its dark head flecked white and topped with tiny spines.
spinyhead-blenny.tip: Scan the upper faces of star and brain coral up close. Hold still and it darts out for plankton, then backs into its hole.

splendid-toadfish.name: Splendid toadfish
splendid-toadfish.description: Flat-headed, white-striped, yellow-finned, and found nowhere on earth but Cozumel.
splendid-toadfish.tip: It sits far back under ledges. Light the gap without crowding it and it will hold.

split-crown-feather-duster.name: Split-crown feather duster
split-crown-feather-duster.description: A small feather duster whose crown parts into two half circles, often banded maroon and white, rising from a tube in coral.
split-crown-feather-duster.tip: Move slowly and keep your shadow off it, and it stays open for a close look.

sponge-brittle-star.name: Sponge brittle star
sponge-brittle-star.description: Long, thin, spiny arms in purple, pink or red, with a dark stripe, draped over sponges and sea fans.
sponge-brittle-star.tip: Check the surface of large sponges, best at night, when the arms reach out to feed.

spot-winged-comb-jelly.name: Spot-winged comb jelly
spot-winged-comb-jelly.description: A clear comb jelly with two broad, flapping lobes, each marked with a dark brown spot.
spot-winged-comb-jelly.tip: Look for it in blue water on a safety stop. It can’t sting, and it swims by beating its lobes.

spotfin-butterflyfish.name: Spotfin butterflyfish
spotfin-butterflyfish.description: White with a yellow trailing edge and a dark bar through the eye.
spotfin-butterflyfish.tip: Look along the reef’s sandy edge at dusk, when pairs come out to feed.

spottail-pinfish.name: Spottail pinfish
spottail-pinfish.description: A silver, flat-sided porgy with one bold black spot on top of the tail base.
spottail-pinfish.tip: Look over sand and rubble by jetties and inshore reefs, where small groups pick at the bottom. Hang still and they come close.

spotted-cleaner-shrimp.name: Spotted cleaner shrimp
spotted-cleaner-shrimp.description: A glass shrimp saddled with white and purple, living inside a stinging anemone.
spotted-cleaner-shrimp.tip: It advertises by waving. Watch one work a fish and you have seen the reef’s whole economy.

spotted-drum.name: Spotted drum
spotted-drum.description: Black-and-white, with an absurdly long first fin the juveniles wave like a ribbon.
spotted-drum.tip: Check the shaded floor of a swim-through; it circles the same small patch all day.

spotted-eagle-ray.name: Spotted eagle ray
spotted-eagle-ray.description: Black wings freckled with white, flying past in open water with a whip of a tail.
spotted-eagle-ray.tip: Look out into the blue at the start of the dive. They pass through and don’t stay.

spotted-goatfish.name: Spotted goatfish
spotted-goatfish.description: A pale goatfish with three dark blotches along the side and two chin barbels, rooting through sand at the reef edge.
spotted-goatfish.tip: Watch the puffs of sand it raises. Opportunists such as bar jacks and wrasses often trail it for anything it flushes.

spotted-moray.name: Spotted moray
spotted-moray.description: White peppered with dark spots, usually one head poking from the rubble.
spotted-moray.tip: Look into rubble and wreck gaps rather than the open reef face. Keep your hands out of the holes.

spotted-scorpionfish.name: Spotted scorpionfish
spotted-scorpionfish.description: Invisible until it moves: a lump of reef with venomous spines along its back.
spotted-scorpionfish.tip: This is why you never put a hand down to steady yourself. Look before you touch.

spotted-sea-hare.name: Spotted sea hare
spotted-sea-hare.description: A soft, olive to tan slug with black rings scattered over its body, grazing algae in the shallows.
spotted-sea-hare.tip: Disturbed, it squirts purple ink, so keep your hands back and let it graze.

spotted-snake-eel.name: Spotted snake eel
spotted-snake-eel.description: A long, thick eel with a pointed snout and rows of dark spots along a cream-colored body, usually seen as a head and neck poking from the sand, or crawling across it.
spotted-snake-eel.tip: Look over sand and seagrass at dusk and on night dives. Keep your distance and your hands to yourself; if crowded it backs into the sand.

spotted-spiny-lobster.name: Spotted spiny lobster
spotted-spiny-lobster.description: A dark, purple-brown lobster covered in white spots, with striped legs, deep inside reef holes.
spotted-spiny-lobster.tip: Shine a light into deep cracks; it sits farther back than the Caribbean spiny lobster.

spotted-trunkfish.name: Spotted trunkfish
spotted-trunkfish.description: A white box covered in black dots, sculling along on two small fins.
spotted-trunkfish.tip: Its shell means it cannot bend, so it turns its whole body, which makes it a slow, comic swimmer.

squirrelfish.name: Squirrelfish
squirrelfish.description: Red and silver with huge night-adapted eyes, tucked into a hole by day.
squirrelfish.tip: Red goes gray at depth without a light, so hold a torch on it to see the color.

staghorn-coral.name: Staghorn coral
staghorn-coral.description: Dense thickets of finger-thick branches, and a nursery for everything small.
staghorn-coral.tip: Fragile and slow-growing. Keep your fins high; a kick takes years back.

star-horseshoe-worm.name: Star horseshoe worm
star-horseshoe-worm.description: A tube worm with a bright orange or red crown in a horseshoe spiral and a stacked, star-edged lid at the center.
star-horseshoe-worm.tip: Scan coral heads up close; it hides fast, so approach slowly and stay low.

stinker-sponge.name: Stinker sponge
stinker-sponge.description: Rounded tan to brown lumps covered in a fine net of raised points, with a few dark openings on top.
stinker-sponge.tip: Named for the garlic smell it gives off out of the water. Below the surface, look for small shrimp and brittle stars in its crevices.

stoplight-parrotfish.name: Stoplight parrotfish
stoplight-parrotfish.description: A heavy beaked grazer: green and gold as an adult, mottled red as a youngster.
stoplight-parrotfish.tip: Move slowly near coral heads and let the color find you.

stovepipe-sponge.name: Stovepipe sponge
stovepipe-sponge.description: Long pale tubes standing well off the wall, tall enough to swim alongside.
stovepipe-sponge.tip: A wall species. On a drift these are the landmark you use to judge how fast you are going.

striped-parrotfish.name: Striped parrotfish
striped-parrotfish.description: Young ones and females are white with three dark stripes; terminal males turn blue-green with salmon and yellow marks.
striped-parrotfish.tip: The striped ones graze in loose schools in the shallows and seagrass. Drift alongside and watch them work the rock.

sun-anemone.name: Sun anemone
sun-anemone.description: A flat carpet of short, stubby tentacles, green to tan, spread wide on shallow reef rock.
sun-anemone.tip: It can sting bare skin. Look among the tentacles for the small shrimp that often lives in it.

sun-anemone-shrimp.name: Sun anemone shrimp
sun-anemone-shrimp.description: A tiny see-through shrimp freckled with brown and white dots, perched among a sun anemone’s tentacles.
sun-anemone-shrimp.tip: Hover over each sun anemone and scan it slowly; the shrimp gives itself away when it moves.

sunshinefish.name: Sunshinefish
sunshinefish.description: A small chromis of deeper reefs. The young are bright yellow above and lavender below, and adults turn olive with a pale belly.
sunshinefish.tip: Look along deep walls and slopes below about 15 meters. The yellow juveniles stand out against the coral.

symmetrical-brain-coral.name: Symmetrical brain coral
symmetrical-brain-coral.description: Tighter, more even ridges than its grooved cousin, in flatter domes.
symmetrical-brain-coral.tip: The valleys hold tiny life. Put a light in one instead of swimming past.

tarpon.name: Tarpon
tarpon.description: A slab of living chrome, up to two meters, hanging in a wreck’s lee.
tarpon.tip: Shield your light against your chest on a night dive and let them work the edge of everyone else’s.

three-rowed-sea-cucumber.name: Three-rowed sea cucumber
three-rowed-sea-cucumber.description: A firm, warty cucumber in tan, orange or brown, dotted with dark chocolate spots, on sand and seagrass.
three-rowed-sea-cucumber.tip: Watch it sift the sand with its feeding tentacles, and leave it on the bottom.

threespot-damselfish.name: Threespot damselfish
threespot-damselfish.description: A small brown farmer with a black spot at the tail, guarding its patch of algae.
threespot-damselfish.tip: It will charge a diver ten times its size. That is a display, and it always stops.

tiger-grouper.name: Tiger grouper
tiger-grouper.description: Slanted tiger bars over a long body, very often parked at a cleaning station.
tiger-grouper.tip: Find the cleaning station and you find the grouper, mouth open and holding still.

tiger-shark.name: Tiger shark
tiger-shark.description: A big, blunt-snouted shark with dark vertical bars along its flanks that fade with age.
tiger-shark.tip: On a provisioned shark dive, follow the operator’s briefing exactly; anywhere else, treat it as an unplanned encounter: stay calm, keep it in view and end the dive.

tobaccofish.name: Tobaccofish
tobaccofish.description: A slim little sea bass with a broad orange-brown stripe low on its side and dark saddles across a pale back, hunting low over sand and rubble.
tobaccofish.tip: Look where the reef breaks up into sand patches. Settle a few meters off and it goes back to hunting in the open.

tomtate.name: Tomtate
tomtate.description: A slim silver grunt with a yellow-bronze stripe along each side and a dark spot at the base of the tail.
tomtate.tip: Schools gather over patch reefs and wrecks. Hold your depth beside the school and it will flow around you.

true-tulip.name: True tulip
true-tulip.description: A smooth, spindle-shaped snail shell, cream to tan or orange, with dark brown blotches and many thin dark lines spiraling around each whorl, on sand and seagrass.
true-tulip.tip: Look for its trail across the sand. It hunts other snails and clams, so give it room and watch from above.

trumpetfish.name: Trumpetfish
trumpetfish.description: A long tube of a fish that hangs head-down among sea rods, pretending to be one.
trumpetfish.tip: Scan vertical shapes in a soft-coral stand. It is hiding in plain sight.

turtle-grass.name: Turtle grass
turtle-grass.description: Ribbon meadows on the sand flats where the reef’s next generation grows up.
turtle-grass.tip: Hover, don’t stand. Every fin-print in a seagrass bed lasts for months.

twospot-cardinalfish.name: Twospot cardinalfish
twospot-cardinalfish.description: A small red cardinalfish with large eyes, one round dark spot under the rear dorsal fin and another at the base of the tail.
twospot-cardinalfish.tip: Look under ledges and in dark recesses by day, or hovering in the open on a night dive. Spots, not bars, tell it apart.

upside-down-jellyfish.name: Upside-down jellyfish
upside-down-jellyfish.description: A jellyfish lying bell-down on the bottom, farming sunlight with its tentacles up.
upside-down-jellyfish.tip: Common in shallow, sheltered bays. Don’t kneel on one; they do sting.

variegated-sea-urchin.name: Variegated sea urchin
variegated-sea-urchin.description: A round urchin with short spines in green, white, purple or red, often holding bits of seagrass and shell over itself.
variegated-sea-urchin.tip: Look in seagrass beds; it wears that debris as a sunshade, so leave its cover in place.

vase-sponge.name: Vase sponge
vase-sponge.description: A wide bell-shaped vase, reddish brown to purple outside and paler within, the wall rough with fine points.
vase-sponge.tip: Peek over the rim without touching it. Small fish and shrimp shelter in the bowl.

vermilion-snapper.name: Vermilion snapper
vermilion-snapper.description: A slim rose-red snapper with a forked tail, fine blue lines along the upper back and short yellow streaks below, schooling over deep reefs and wrecks.
vermilion-snapper.tip: Expect them on deeper ledges and wrecks, often past 25 meters. Watch the open water above the structure, where the school hangs.

wahoo.name: Wahoo
wahoo.description: A long, slim, steel-blue fish with faint vertical bars on the flank, a pointed snout and a mouth full of sharp, flat teeth.
wahoo.tip: Look in open water beside walls and drop-offs. It is fast and wary, so do not chase it. A still diver at the edge of the blue sees the most.

west-indian-sea-egg.name: West Indian sea egg
west-indian-sea-egg.description: A big, rounded urchin with a dark body bristling with short white spines, on seagrass and rubble.
west-indian-sea-egg.tip: The short spines barely prick, but leave it where it is; it’s a key grazer of seagrass beds.

whale-shark.name: Whale shark
whale-shark.description: A checkerboard the size of a bus, filter-feeding at the surface in season.
whale-shark.tip: Never touch or block its path, and stay clear of the tail. Local rules set the distance.

white-encrusting-zoanthid.name: White encrusting zoanthid
white-encrusting-zoanthid.description: A cream to tan mat of short, crowded polyps spreading over shallow rock and dead coral.
white-encrusting-zoanthid.tip: Look in the surge zone of shallow reefs, and don’t touch it; its mucus carries a strong toxin.

white-grunt.name: White grunt
white-grunt.description: Pale blue and yellow head lines, with a flash of orange inside the mouth.
white-grunt.tip: They do grunt. You can hear a school through the water on a quiet dive.

white-margate.name: White margate
white-margate.description: A large, deep-bodied grunt that is plain pearly gray all over, with thick lips and no stripes.
white-margate.tip: Often alone or in small groups along sand channels near the reef. Hover low and it keeps feeding on the bottom.

whitespotted-filefish.name: Whitespotted filefish
whitespotted-filefish.description: A big, deep-bodied filefish in orange or brown that can flash a coat of white spots in seconds.
whitespotted-filefish.tip: Often seen in pairs nibbling sponges and sea fans. Swim parallel to them rather than straight in and they may stay in view.

yellow-goatfish.name: Yellow goatfish
yellow-goatfish.description: Silvery white with a yellow stripe from eye to a bright yellow forked tail, resting in loose schools by day.
yellow-goatfish.tip: Watch one feed over sand: two chin barbels sweep the bottom, and wrasses often follow for the leftovers.

yellow-jack.name: Yellow jack
yellow-jack.description: A silvery jack with a yellowish cast and yellow-tinged fins, with no dark spot on the gill cover.
yellow-jack.tip: Usually alone or in small groups along the reef edge. Hold still and it may swing in for a closer look.

yellow-pencil-coral.name: Yellow pencil coral
yellow-pencil-coral.description: Dense thickets of thin yellow to tan branches with rounded tips, spreading across the reef slope.
yellow-pencil-coral.tip: Small fish shelter between the branches. Hover above the thicket and look down into it.

yellow-stingray.name: Yellow stingray
yellow-stingray.description: A small, round, mottled ray that lies still in the sand between coral heads.
yellow-stingray.tip: It carries a venomous spine at the tail. Look before you settle onto sand and come down slowly; this is the one most divers land on.

yellow-tube-sponge.name: Yellow tube sponge
yellow-tube-sponge.description: Clusters of yellow chimneys standing off the wall, each one an open pipe.
yellow-tube-sponge.tip: A reliable color marker in poor visibility. You can see the yellow from far off.

yellowbelly-hamlet.name: Yellowbelly hamlet
yellowbelly-hamlet.description: Dark blue-brown on the back, with a yellow belly, yellow pelvic fins and a yellow tail.
yellowbelly-hamlet.tip: Hamlets keep to a small patch. Find one near a coral head and wait rather than following it.

yellowcheek-wrasse.name: Yellowcheek wrasse
yellowcheek-wrasse.description: A long wrasse with a broad blue-black band along the upper side, a yellow-green back and yellow on the head and cheek.
yellowcheek-wrasse.tip: A fish of deeper slopes and walls, rarely shallower than 15 meters. Watch along the reef edge where it forages over rubble.

yellowfin-grouper.name: Yellowfin grouper
yellowfin-grouper.description: Blotched red or gray with a yellow rim to the pectoral fins, out on the wall.
yellowfin-grouper.tip: The yellow fin edge is the only reliable mark. Its body color changes as you watch.

yellowfin-mojarra.name: Yellowfin mojarra
yellowfin-mojarra.description: A deep-bodied silver fish with faint dusky bars and bright yellow fins on the belly, over sand and seagrass close to shore.
yellowfin-mojarra.tip: Watch it feed: the mouth shoots out like a tube to suck prey from the sand. Hover above the bottom so you do not stir it up.

yellowhead-jawfish.name: Yellowhead jawfish
yellowhead-jawfish.description: A pale fish hovering upright over its burrow, dropping in tail-first when startled.
yellowhead-jawfish.tip: Settle on the sand at a distance and wait. It comes back up within a minute.

yellowhead-wrasse.name: Yellowhead wrasse
yellowhead-wrasse.description: Yellow-headed adults and lemon-yellow youngsters, never still for a moment.
yellowhead-wrasse.tip: Too fast to chase. Pick a coral head, hold, and let it work its way back around to you.

yellowline-goby.name: Yellowline goby
yellowline-goby.description: A small dark goby with a bright yellow line from the snout along the upper side, living on and inside tube sponges.
yellowline-goby.tip: Peer into the mouth of a tube or barrel sponge. Several may perch on the rim and slip inside if you come too close.

yellowmouth-grouper.name: Yellowmouth grouper
yellowmouth-grouper.description: A brown to tan grouper with small dark spots and blotches, and yellow around the corners of the mouth.
yellowmouth-grouper.tip: Hangs near ledges and wall overhangs. Approach calmly and it will often let you watch from a few meters.

yellownose-goby.name: Yellownose goby
yellownose-goby.description: A tiny cleaner goby with a bright yellow bar on the snout and a yellow stripe from eye to tail, found on living coral in the southeastern Caribbean.
yellownose-goby.tip: Watch the top of brain and star coral heads. Fish waiting to be cleaned will show you where it works.

yellowtail-damselfish.name: Yellowtail damselfish
yellowtail-damselfish.description: Dark body, bright yellow tail; the young ones are speckled with electric blue.
yellowtail-damselfish.tip: The juveniles are the show. Look for blue sparks over fire coral in the shallows.

yellowtail-hamlet.name: Yellowtail hamlet
yellowtail-hamlet.description: A small bass, dark blue-black to brown all over except for a bright yellow tail, hovering close to the coral.
yellowtail-hamlet.tip: The yellow tail is the whole field mark. Settle near a coral head and it will go on hunting in front of you.

yellowtail-parrotfish.name: Yellowtail parrotfish
yellowtail-parrotfish.description: Young adults are mottled gray with dark-edged scales and reddish fins; terminal males are green with a yellow tail and a black spot at the pectoral base.
yellowtail-parrotfish.tip: Often grazes in small groups over shallow rock and seagrass. Approach low and slow and listen for the crunch of its beak.

yellowtail-snapper.name: Yellowtail snapper
yellowtail-snapper.description: Silver schools ruled by one bright yellow stripe running out into the tail.
yellowtail-snapper.tip: Look into the blue beyond the reef instead of only looking down.
